Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? A Russian deserter who was tricked to sign up for the war told ‘The Insider’ how he was nearly killed by his own Russian troops at the front, next to a pit with 20–30 bodies. He was badly wounded when his commander sent him to pick some vodka, and nearly bled out with no assistance. It was after this experience that he decided to run off. Anton (not his real name) had no intention of joining the army whatsoever. But in the fall of 2023, he went out to a shop, and a police patrol stopped him to check his documents. Anton didn’t have his ID with him and the cops took him to the police station. They put his data into a computer and told him he had an outstanding mobilization summons and would be going to the front in 3 days. They threatened that he would have huge problems for trying to skip mobilization — but there could be a way around: he could go to the enlistment office and ask to sign the contract voluntarily. The cops told him that if he signed the contract (as opposed to being mobilized), he would be able to pick an “easy” job, like helping out in a hospital. Anton came home horrified. The idea of improving his odds to get an “easy” military job as opposed to being sent to the front as mobilized seemed reasonable. He decided that if he anyway would be mobilized, he’d better become a contractor. He signed the contract on Saturday, and on Tuesday he was already sent to a unit. And — surprise, surprise! — he was sent to an assault company. A week later he was already at the front line. That was a shock for Anton: “A week ago I was sitting at home, watching videos, working, leading a normal life, and now I'm at the trenches in Ukraine.” It didn’t take long at the front for commanders to start sending people to assaults. His unit’s goal was to take a position at the edge of a village. But to get there, the soldiers had to run over 500 meters of an open space. From the Ukrainian side, that open space was controlled by a machine gun that was able to take out up to 100 people at once. The only cover a group could take was a damaged tank stranded in the middle. The commander told the assault teams to take cover and dig an outpost near the tank, to create a position from which they would be able to move further forward. Anton says it was an idiotic plan: there was no difference whether you had to run 250 or 500 meters, after 30 seconds in an open area you would be a “toast”. The commander began sending groups of 5: on the first day, 4 groups were sent, all 20 ended up dead. No one could even reach that tank. The next day another 20 people got killed. Anton says, Ukrainians have 15–20 various drones — both killer drones and reconnaissance drones — in the air at any time, day or night. The drones see any movement immediately. “It felt like the Ukrainian Armed Forces had a 50-fold advantage in drones,” he says. Then the commanders decided to send only 2 people at once. One group managed to reach the tank and dug in, and the propagandists on TV immediately began reporting that “the village was taken.” But the Russian troops still haven’t even reached it. The commander, a former security guard from a supermarket, dreamed of seeing himself on Channel 1, to feel like a hero warrior. So, he kept sending one group after the other to the slaughter, demanding that they move forward towards the village. The group that dug in near the tank managed to survive, but they needed ammunition, food, water — so, more people were sent in to deliver supplies, and they kept being shot by the Ukrainian fire. Anton says that about 70 people died there in a week, near that tank. Anton says that the worst wasn’t even the gunfire — the worst was when you leave the dugout and are completely exposed, and you realize that at any second you can be killed. “I went out to the toilet, went back 30 seconds later, and at the place where I was, 2 mortars hit” he recalls. Sometimes the Ukrainian drone operators made errors and the drones fell down, then the commanders sent Russian soldiers into the minefields to pick them up. A task from which one is unlikely to return, because no one has maps of the minefields, the mines are just thrown in, where it falls, that’s where it falls. “You have a patch of land, 4 drones fly around it. They drop something, as soon as they fly away — the next 4 are already flying. And in the distance, there are probably 5 more, coordinating fire by mortars and artillery,” explains Anton. If a drone noticed you, you aren’t allowed to hide back in a dugout — because the operator sees a glowing dot, and suddenly it disappears: it means the person has gone somewhere. Then a precise hit arrives — and minimum 5 people in the dugout will be dead. Anton says that in 2 weeks, only 15–20 people were left from 250 soldiers that arrived, and from them 10 people were the commanders and non-combat clerks. Most of the soldiers were contractors, only a few were “mobilized”. From the losses, about 40% are dead, the rest are wounded. About 50% of the wounded are without legs or arms — disabled for life. “When I arrived, that village was still more or less intact. 3 weeks later it was just ruins. Heaps of corpses…” recalls Anton. He survived because he was part of the “evacuation team” — and he refused to go in the assaults, saying he would continue performing the task he was assigned to do. He was still going to the position near the tank, but his job was to pull the wounded, not carry provisions or stay in the dugout. Although Anton didn’t do any specific medical training, he had to perform an amputation in the field. This was like a horror movie. He pulled a guy who was lying wounded in the field for 3 days. The guy managed to apply tourniquets to wounds on his arm and leg, but after these 3 days his arm began to rot. The medics told him on the radio he had to amputate the arm. Anton injected the guy with all sedatives he could find and chopped the arm with an axe. It took him 4 attempts to get through the flesh and bones, then he had to treat the stump and bandage it. “I didn't sleep for two days after that,” Anton says. “When we were loading him [for evacuation], he was still alive, and he also made it to the first line alive. I don't know what happened to him after that.” Another guy that Anton pulled out had part of his jaw torn off, his arm up to the shoulder and half a leg. The commander was pissed off about it: "I don't need this, now I have to do something for one more person." A day later the injured guy was already begging to die, realizing he wouldn’t survive. At the end, he bled to death. The dead were rarely pulled out from the field. It was too much trouble to even attempt it. Once Anton had to hide from a drone and crawled into an old dugout, and realized he was crawling on top of liquified bodies in uniform. The bodies were there for already 3–4 months. There was one guy in the unit of about 18–19, he was a draftee (all Russian men have to serve a 1-year compulsory military service, but the draftees are not supposed to be sent to Ukraine to the war). That guy was also tricked into signing a contract — in the military enlistment office where he arrived as a draftee, they simply gave him some papers to sign, and he signed, not realizing what it was. “A week and a half later, he was already at the front line,” says Anton. The guy’s family sent a letter, complaining to the prosecutor's office that he was forced to sign the contract. The battalion commander was furious about it and gave the order to “sort him out.” The teenage soldier was sent into an attack and killed within a week. Anton says his commander was constantly drunk. One day the commander ordered him to pick another drone from the headquarters — Anton argued it was unnecessary to do it at night, as they had a spare drone they could use, and at night it’s really easy to see a person on thermal visors. But the commander insisted. Anton managed to get to the headquarters, where they gave him a drone and a package “for the commander”. Anton looked inside the bag, and there were bottles of vodka and cognac. The commander sent him to get the alcohol for him and he didn’t care it was deadly dangerous. On the way back, Anton heard a drone over him and immediately an explosive dropped on him. Anton was wounded and couldn’t walk, but he realized he still had both his arms and legs. He threw away the bag with vodka and crawled into the nearest basement, got on the radio, said that he was wounded and asked for evacuation. They responded it was too dangerous to try to get him. After 20 minutes, he realized that he was bleeding out. “I was shaking all over, tremors, I definitely lost a liter of blood,” says Anton. He decided to crawl, and managed to make it to the line where he could be picked up — out of the firing range. Anton says that ”almost everyone drinks” at the front line — or they are using cheap drugs (“salts”). The commanders also steal strong pain killers from the first aid kits given to soldiers and use those. If a soldier refuses to follow orders, he isn’t sent to a military court for prosecution but simply shot by the commander’s underlings — his arms and legs are taped to a tree, and he’s shot at a point blank range. Sometimes a person may be dressed in 2 bulletproof vests and then shot at with a machine gun, his ribs get broken and he slowly dies. Or he’s shot at through a helmet — such shots take off the whole skull. Anton says that 2 soldiers in his unit were liquidated like this, for not following orders — they refused to go in an attack, because all previous groups were killed. Anton himself nearly got shot — when in the field, he noticed a drone in the sky and went back, but took to the left and ended up in a neighboring unit. That unit was looking for a mobilized soldier on the run and took Anton for the deserter. He was tied to a tree and about to be shot, there was a hole nearby, where 20–30 bodies were already lying. He was saved by a radio message that the runaway soldier was found. Do the Russian soldiers realize that Russia’s war in Ukraine is evil? Do they blame Putin for that? Nobody among the Russian troops at the front says things like "let's go overthrow Putin,” states Anton. “Of course, they say that he [Putin] has started some kind of screwup that no one needs.” ”Even the ‘patriots’ when they arrive, very soon start saying, ‘What are we even doing here, why the heck do we need this?’” “There are some ‘ultra patriots’, but they do not survive for long, because they are the first to run ahead and the first to get killed.” “There was this guy, 54 years old, his wife had cancer. He came not even for the money, but because he needed the benefits for a serviceman's family, so his wife could get the cancer treatment. He was saying: ‘I know that people get killed here, I made my choice. If I get killed, at least my wife will get 5 million ruble, she will get the treatment, the children will live well." That guy lived in a small regional town. His monthly salary was 35,000 ruble (about USD$400). He had 3 kids, his wife was sick. He saw it as his only option to help the wife and the kids. “You are not a human being there at all,” says Anton. He fears what is going to happen in Russia when all these people with the broken psyche come back. “When these people come back from the war with blood on their hands, with a broken psyche, who were in the same companies, detachments and so on, they will start to form groups, and these smaller groups will start to form bigger groups...” Anton says that plenty of weapons are transported back to Russia in bags with dead bodies — pulled into parts and hidden in these bags. An AK-47 costs about 40,000 ruble in Russia now ($460). Anton says that if the Russian soldiers are being utilized at the same rate as at his part of the front, Russia has suffered about 400,000 losses by now — killed and badly wounded. Anton says that no one signing an army contract should hope they’d come back with the money — because they won’t. At best, they can hope to come back home with the money in case of a serious wound — but then, “Do you want your mother to be wiping off your butt for the rest of your life?” “If you think there are some Nazis there... There are no Nazis, there are ordinary people. If you, so to say, go and kill your neighbor, would you be able to live with that for the rest of your life?” “This war is not worth it. This is not a war for the Fatherland, this is not a war for justice, not a war for freedom — this is a war for the complete bullshit. A war for the grandfather who is so crazy that he went and killed hundreds of thousands of people for nothing, just like that.” “You are not liberating anyone. He [the crazy grandfather] himself doesn't believe that he is liberating anyone, he doesn't give a f**k about all this — and even less about you.” What can the Russian men do to avoid being sent to the war? “Better run,” says Anton. ”No money? Take out loans and use that money to escape.” Anton himself deserted after getting wounded. Yesterday, Putin signed a decree raising the federal payout on signing the army contact to 400,000 rub. ($4,600) — it’s nearly twice as much as the state was paying before. Regions are also raising their payouts — St. Petersburg just raised it’s top-up to 1.8 million, and Moscow already lifted it to 1.9 million rub. ($22,000). Russia is running out of volunteers, so the prices for cannon fodder are rising. Putin is too scared to do another mobilization and force people to kill and die, because he knows how unpopular this war really is.

When will Putin stop? If Putin were locked in a prison cell, this madness of a full-scale war in Ukraine and constant Russian threats would certainly stop. Failing that (which would be only possible through an internal coup), Putin would be forced to stop if he could no longer draft enough soldiers to send to the war in Ukraine or was unable to equip them with weapons. Willingly, Putin might stop if he were given an appearance of a victory in Ukraine: something that he could announce to the Russian populace as a triumph. For 2.5 years of the full-scale war, the Russian populace had been diligently suppressed to the level where they don’t dare to speak up — they can’t even verbalize their dismay with being “best friends” with the North Korea, which for decades has been the butt of every joke about backward dictatorships. The Russian people have to swallow their nationalistic chauvinism and display satisfaction about “strategic alliance” of Putin and Kim Jong Un. Despite numerous failures in Ukraine, Putin’s propaganda still claims that Putin is “winning” — and that they “haven’t really started yet”, and the Russian population accepts it as the indisputable truth. So, whatever Putin decides to announce as a “victory” in Ukraine, wouldn’t be disputed by the population — no matter how shameful the conditions of the deal would be for Russia. Putin’s refusal to give up isn’t because of him being afraid to lose power — it’s purely an obsession. Putin made a mistake and refuses to admit it, pretending “all is going according to plan”. Alas, the likelihood of Putin’s getting to his senses and starting to make decisions that are rational (i.e. good for Russia and Russians) isn’t high. Most likely, he would do anything to continue the war in Ukraine, hoping he’d have a chance to prevail if his army were able to last another few months — ad nauseam. Meanwhile, Russia’s economy is in deep trouble, which even the Russian officials can no longer deny. In words of the first deputy chairman of the Central Bank Vladimir Chistyukhin, the system is on the brink of a “collapse”, because of Russia’s incorrigible dependency on import. In other words, if Russia can’t import goods and services, its economy would crash within months. The latest western sanctions severely impacted Russia’s ability to pay for imported goods via legitimate payment methods, and the Russian Central Bank is unable to bypass this block, desperately researching crutch options, including barter and use of cryptocurrencies. Putin is willing to bet Russia’s present and future on his neo-USSR project. And he is convinced that Ukraine is ‘the Holy Grail’ that would tip the scales in his favor. But for that, he needs the whole of Ukraine — he can’t allow any part of Ukraine, especially Kyiv, to stay out of his grasp. He needs Odesa, he needs Mykolaiv, he needs Kharkiv. He can’t get it by force — not for the lack of trying. Putin is prepared to try to get it by other means, and his preference would be to turn Ukrainians against their government, to instigate an “anti-Maidan” coup, and install a puppet government to rule over Ukraine. That in his view is the most promising and cost effective course of action, and that’s why anyone in the west willing to sell out to Russia gets paid handsomely — Jason Hinkle recently bragged he bought a plane from his earnings on X-Twitter: Kremlin bots promote threads through incessant commenting and reposts, and Musk pays out the cash. Simple scheme. Just remember: Putin’s goal is the destroy the USA, EU and NATO. Even if the war in Ukraine stops, Putin won’t stop the war against the West. Only a change of regime in Russia can stop it.

Are you surprised by the result of the large drone attack on Moscow during the Kursk incursion? Sunrise over Moscow this morning — Ukraine launched a massive nighttime kamikaze drone attack on multiple locations in Russia, including Moscow, Rostov, Bryansk, and Belgorod. Moscow suburb of Podolsk, 20 miles south of the Kremlin, had drones flying over. ”All 10 drones have been destroyed,” reported the Moscow mayor — we just need to wait for the information from Ukraine to find out whether some of them were destroyed by oil depots or other military targets. The Russian ministry of defence reported that they shot down 45 Ukrainian drones over Russia last night. In Novoshakhtinsk, drones destroyed Russian S-300 long range surface-to-air missile system. The Russian internet is flooded this morning with videos of drones flying over the Central Russia. People who made the videos sound really concerned — especially when they see a drone exploding. Also today, Ukrainian drones attacked a strategic airfield in Russia's Murmansk region — that’s beyond the Arctic Circle, 2,000 kilometers away from Ukraine. It is from this airfield that planes that carry cruise missiles attacking Ukrainian cities are flying from. Russians had to remove their planes from near the front line for safety, but even 2,000 km away from Ukraine is no longer safe for the military targets that Ukrainians want to hit. Meanwhile, in the Russian town of Proletarsk in Rostov region, the fire at the oil depot, caused by 2 Ukrainian drones, is burning uncontrollably for the 4th day. Smoke from the fire is already visible from space, the plume stretches for 160 km. All to no avail. The burning oil depot is the strategic fuel reserve, which contained 2.5 million barrels of petrol and diesel, worth USD $500 million. A third of the 76 tanks have already burned. It’s expected the fire will keep burning for another week. Meanwhile, the territory of the Kursk region under control of the Ukrainian forces expanded to 1,263 square kilometers, and the number of settlements under Ukraine’s control increased to 93, reported Ukrainian commander-in-chief Syrskyi. Reportedly, up to 3,000 Russian soldiers are now surrounded and cut off from supplies by the Ukrainian troops, after 3 bridges were destroyed on the Seym River. It’s likely that Ukrainians will have to deal with mass surrenders in the coming days. Vladimir Putin, who didn’t say anything about Kursk invasion since the first days when it was treated as a “raid”, today mentioned Kursk. Putin again spoke about Kursk in the context of “terrorist activities”, looking lost and clutching his hands in a tight grip. (Video in the comments below.) Apparently, in Donbas and “Novorossia” (that’s how Putin calls occupied Ukrainian regions) it’s also all “terrorists” that Russia is fighting against. 42 million terrorists. Against 140 million Russians who just want to be left alone. Putin’s chances don’t look good.

How does Putin think he will win against the rest of the world? This cover of “The Spectator” is dated October 2016. Putin has just increased 10 times the reach of Kremlin propaganda among western viewers, compared to the start of 2024 — and you can be sure they are not going to stop there. A network of pro-Kremlin bots, nicknamed Doppelgänger by western analysts, has sharply increased its reach among social media users in different countries, reported ‘The Insider’. This shocking fact was discovered by analysts of ‘AntibotNavalny’, who reviewed the reach of cleverly designed tweets, promoting Kremlin narratives. Analysts came to the conclusion that this level of coverage of the bot network was achieved thanks to texts generated by artificial intelligence. ‘Doppelgänger’ is a network of accounts disseminating Kremlin narratives aimed at Western audiences, including propaganda videos, caricatures of Western leaders, and links to “journalistic” articles from websites created by the Kremlin. Doppelgänger uses the same method as fraudulent websites that try to steal your money — only the Kremlin tries to steal your thoughts. So, Putin is massively escalating its hybrid war against the West. Russia is waging the war against the whole western civilization. For Putin, it’s the war for world domination. And every one of us is under attack.

Where are Russian Kursk reinforcements coming from? Reportedly, Russia is scrubbing for soldiers and pulling anyone, to send them to Kursk, where the Ukrainian army invaded on August 6, 2024. Troops are transferred to the Kursk region from Kaliningrad — which is actually the area surrounded by NATO countries. Shows you how much Putin is really worried about “NATO aggression” — he’s leaving all other areas near border bare, to throw soldiers into the Ukrainian meat grinder. Some troops and heavy equipment are also being transferred from the Kharkiv region of Ukraine, where the Russian army tried to advance. 500 Russians who refused the military service on the base of “conscience objection” and health issues were grabbed in St. Petersburg region and flown to Kursk. Some of them have mental health issues. “They took a man with category “D” [unfit for service], plus a man of about 70 years old who could barely walk, and another man without an eye…”, a relative of one of the soldiers said. By the morning of August 13, about 150 people were delivered to a military training ground near Kursk. Another 300 “refuseniks” were taken in another direction. Several soldiers with minor concussions were taken away from the hospital in Kursk the day before. According to the witness, "everyone understands" that the soldiers are being taken somewhere near the border to fight in battles again. Conscripts in the Kursk region are being forced to sign contracts with the army, mothers of two draftees reported. According to them, there are currently about 150 conscripts in one of the military units in the Kursk region who are to be sent to the front as contract soldiers. (Conscripts who serve the compulsory 1-year service aren’t supposed to be in combat.) The conscripts are told that they would be "cleaning the area after the stormtroopers" and promised payments of 4,500 ruble per day (about USD $50). According to one of the mothers, her son was told: "You will go there anyway, but now [if you sign the contract], we will pay you the combat fee… And if you do not agree, then you will be sent to the military court — and still have to go to fight, you won’t have any choice." $50 per day for a most certain death within days. Life of Putin’s soldiers isn’t worth much. Same story is reported from the Murmansk region: conscripts are being prepped to be sent to Kursk. This includes young conscripts who were drafted last month. This is why the Russian soldiers keep surrendering to Ukrainians en masse. In less than 24 hours, another 100 Russian conscripts surrendered in the Kursk region, reported commander Syrskyi. Hitler, who started the World War 2, was responsible for the deaths of 14-year-olds who were sent to defend besieged Berlin in 1945. Putin, who started this war, will be responsible for the deaths of conscripts who are now being sent to defend the Kursk region. And many of them are already dead. Not everyone manages to surrender.

Why does Ukraine increasingly use its long-range firepower to hit oil refineries and depots deep inside Russia? Last night, another oil depot next to a processing plant was hit in Rostov region of Russia — there are now 2 oil depots on fire: ‘Atlas’ near Molodezhny settlement, which went on fire today, and the one in Proletarsk, which is burning for 11th day. Both oil depots belong to the state strategic reserve and were holding hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fuel. Reportedly, ‘Atlas’ depot was struck by 2 Ukrainian drones: 3 tanks are burning; 2 fire trains are at the scene trying to extinguish the fire. Because of Ukraine’s attacks on oil processing plants and fuel depots, passenger planes in Russia are now put on strict limits: only 30-minute reserve of fuel is allowed per plane per flight. A pilot of a Russian airline complained that it makes flights extremely risky, because in case of a weather front or potential “drone alert” (which happen around Moscow and St. Petersburg airports fairly often), a plane may not have enough fuel to fly around, wait it out in the air or reach another air field. Fuel shortages disturb the Russian military logistics, and “eternal” multi-day fires have massive demoralizing effect on the Russian population.

What do you think of the state of propaganda in Russia right now? For over a decade, the Russian media was permeated with the anti-Ukraine propaganda. After Putin unleashed the full-scale invasion on Ukraine in February 2022, following 8 years of clandestine operations, the covert propaganda in Russia went into the full-on mode as well. A recent story highlighted the state of propaganda in Russia right now — it’s as bad as Hitler’s. Anti-war activists posted poems from the times of Nazi Germany, glorifying Nazism and the Fuhrer (translated to Russian) in an account on Russian ‘VK’ social network — and Z-patriots absolutely loved the poems! Fictional Z-poet ‘Gennady Rakitin’ for a whole year was passing off Nazi poems as his own “patriotic” verses. According to the legend, Rakitin was a 49-year-old graduate of the Moscow State University and a former teacher. The poems he published were supposedly praising the ‘special military operation’, the Motherland, Russians and Putin. The only photo of the Z-poet was created by AI. One of the poems was dedicated to Vladimir Putin and called “The Leader”. Many Russian propaganda outlets reprinted it. In reality, the poem was a translation of “The Fuhrer” by Eberhard Möller, a Nazi who became a member of the NSDAP even before Hitler came to power. “Nameless Stormtrooper,” in which NSDAP member Heinrich Anacker addressed his fellow storm troopers, became “The Nameless Soldier of ‘Wagner’.” To give the story a worthy ending, ‘Gennady Rakitin’ posted his last poem (his own, for a change): “For a long while, Gennady has been mocking Z-verses on the wall, And finally, he drew **** the war." The reaction from Z-community was priceless: one Duma member said he’d “beat up” Rakitin if he met him! The brightness of Russian lawmakers just keeps shining through.

Does the breathtaking rate at which Mariupol has been rebuilt suggest a prosperous future for Eastern Ukraine? Russian journalists can only make videos in Mariupol by shooting from down up. Kremlin propagandists are forbidden to photograph the city from above. But here is how the cheerful new buildings look against the backdrop of neighborhoods destroyed by Putin’s bombs. In 2 years that Russia controls Mariupol, many destroyed buildings in the city have been demolished — without even attempting to get the dead bodies from the basements, where people were hiding from Russian bombs and where they perished. Russians simply excavated the ruins with everything in them and took the crashed remnants to the giant dump outside the city. Tens of thousands of Ukrainians who perished during the 3-month siege of Mariupol will always remain “missing”. Residents of Mariupol (these who managed to survive the Russian siege) are still living in car garages. Like vultures, Russian citizens travel to Mariupol for “cheap deals”, buying up damaged property and evicting the rightful residents. This is the true face of “the Russian world.” This is what Russia looks like in all its glory — only painted facades along the central streets, ruins and destruction hidden from cameras everywhere else. Mariupol is one of Russia’s most heinous war crimes. Without statute of limitations.

How has the element of surprise impacted Ukraine's incursion into the Kursk region? At a meeting with foreign diplomates, Ukraine President Zelenskyy said that Ukrainians kept quiet about the offensive in the Kursk region of Russia because it might have appeared unrealistic. "Just a few months ago, upon hearing that we were planning such an operation in Kursk Oblast, many representatives of the international community would have said that it was unrealistic and it crossed Russia’s main red line,” said Zelenskyy. “This is why nobody had been informed about our preparations. Now the real success speaks for itself: our active defensive actions on the other side of the border and Putin’s inability to protect his territory from our defensive actions of this kind are very telling." Truth is, most likely the Ukrainians kept quiet about the plan to invade Russia because they had experience of their plans leaked to Russians. One of previous operations was reportedly cancelled because Russians found out about the plan, and the big offensive of 2023 didn’t turn out well for Ukraine because Russians knew where the Ukrainian forces planned to attack. Apparently, only commander-in-chief Syrskyi and president Zelenskyy himself, along with a few top generals, knew about the plan. Even the people in the office of the Ukrainian president didn’t know: Syrskyi talked to Zelenskyy 1-to-1. The Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR) didn’t participate in planning the Kursk operation; the army used its own intel. The soldiers of the Ukrainian forces found out about the operation just hours before. In the briefing for foreign diplomates, Zelenskyy explained that right now a huge ideological change is occurring: "The whole naive illusory concept of Russia’s so-called ‘red lines’, which prevailed in some partners’ assessment of the war, crumbled somewhere near Sudzha over these few days." “Now the world sees that it is realistic, that it really works. Not only in the temporarily occupied territory of our country but in the territory of Russia as well. The world sees that everything in this war depends only on courage — our courage, and the courage of our partners,” said Zelenskyy. All we need is courage. And weapons.

Has the Russian ferry Conro Trader sunk near Kerch after an Ukrainian attack struck its flammable cargo, causing a major fire on board and loss of 15 crew? Was the ferry carrying 30 fueled tanks hit by a Ukrainian Long Neptune anti-ship missile? TAP ON THE PHOTO TO VIEW. On August 22, Ukraine hit large Russian ferry “Conro Trader”, with 30 railway carriage tanks of fuel on board, which exploded and the ferry sank. Convenient. No need to try to combat the fire — in the nearby Rostov region, an oil depot with fuel tanks is burning for the 6th day, and over 50 Russian firemen had already been hurt trying to put the fire down, as more and more tanks exploded. By now, the Russian authorities instructed the firemen to stay away from the raging fire, to avoid more casualties. The fire will likely keep going until all the fuel worth USD $0.5 billion burns out. Interestingly, a video of the ferry with fuel tanks aboard was posted online an hour before the Ukrainian ‘Neptune’ missiles hit. (The video in the comments below.) Reportedly, ‘Conro Trader’ was the only ferry that Russia had on the Black Sea, capable of transporting railway carriages. Now Russia has to transport fuel to Crimea by the Kerch bridge (aka Crimean bridge), which they tried to avoid: previously, the bridge was severely damaged because an explosion hit fuel carriages of a train, and the bridge had to be partiality closed down for repairs for months. The Crimean bridge is very close to the port where the ferry sank. Is the Crimean bridge the next target for Ukrainian ‘Neptunes’?

Even though Putin refuses to face the reality, most people surrounding him see the writing on the wall.

Could I buy cheap apartment in Ukraine in their new city, Kursk? The Ukrainian forces haven’t reached the Kursk city as yet — and probably don’t have such a goal. But they have already achieved multiple strategic goals. For the first time during this war, the combat is happening on the territory of Russia on a large scale. Previous raids into the Russian territory by the Russian volunteer corps (made of Russian citizens) that fight on the side of Ukraine didn’t last long and weren’t as deep. This time it’s a proper large-scale military operation with the use of heavy equipment and thousands of troops. Roman Sheremeta, professor of economics at Case Western Reserve University, points out the results that Ukraine had managed to achieve by its Kursk operation: And the added bonus for Ukraine is that now the fighting is on the Russian soil and any devastation will be Russia’s problem.

What types of strategies do you suggest to optimize your Quora usage and increase views? I’ve been writing for the Internet since 1999 — and good content has always been the key. That’s what I found out in my 6+ years of writing for Quora (and wish I knew when I just started): Quora is a great community of thinkers, with over 400 million unique visitors coming to the site every month in search of answers. Was Stalin really that bad, or was he a victim of propaganda? In 1930s, young Mikhail Sholokhov was already a known author in the USSR for his book “Tales of the Don” (1925), depicting his personal experiences during the WWI, the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 and the Civil War. When Stalin’s attack on peasants with the goal of shoveling them into “collective farms” began, Sholokhov lived in the village of Veshenskaya, Rostov region, and could see what was happening with the people. Witnessing the deaths and suffering of peasants, Sholokhov wrote 4 letters to Stalin in hopes of saving people. April 20, 1932: “I saw something that cannot be forgotten till my last days: at night, in the Volokhovsky village of the Lebyazhensky collective farm, in the fierce wind, in the freezing cold, when even dogs were hiding from the frosty weather, families of peasants who were thrown out of their houses had been burning fires in the alleys and sitting near the flames. Children were wrapped in rags and laid on the bare ground, thawed by the fire. A continuous children’s cry stood over the alleys. Why are people being tortured like that? In the Bazkovsky collective farm, a woman with a baby was evicted from her home. She was walking around the village all night, asking to be allowed to warm up with her child. Nobody let her in, fearing that if they do, they themselves would be evicted. By morning, the child froze to death in his mother's arms...” Stalin replied that Sholokhov simply lacked the class consciousness. Yes, Stalin was absolutely evil. It’s not just “propaganda”.

What do you think will happen to Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich who was arrested for alleged spying in Russia? On July 19, 2024, the Regional Court in Yekaterinburg, Russia, sentenced American journalist Evan Gershkovich to 16 years in a maximum security colony. Russian human rights activist Vladimir Osechkin says that possibly he was baited by the FSB, to facilitate his arrest. 32-year-old journalist of WSJ was found guilty of espionage for collecting information about ‘Uralvagonzavod’, which is a factory that makes tanks for the Russian army. The prosecutor asked for an 18-year sentence. Gershkovich pleaded “not guilty” and insisted that he was acting as a journalist, not a spy. The court hearings were held behind closed doors, as the prosecution alleged the information that Gershkovich was getting was a “state secret”. Only the judge, the prosecutor, the defendant and his lawyers were present. Journalists were allowed into the meeting room for a few minutes before the hearing commenced to take photos and videos. Gershkovich, with a shaved head, greeted his colleagues with a smile, but did not answer any questions. Journalists were also allowed into the courtroom for the announcement of the harsh verdict: 16 years in a maximum security prison. Evan Gershkovich was detained on March 29, 2023 in Yekaterinburg, where he arrived for the second time in a month, to continue his investigation for the next story. At the WSJ Gershkovich worked since January 2022 — he joined the respected media just a month before Russia invaded Ukraine. Since then, he authored several key news stories related to Russia and Ukraine. In early March 2023, weeks before his arrest in Russia, he and his colleagues released a story about the growing tensions between the founder of “Wagner” Yevgeny Prigozhin and the Kremlin elites. In particular, the material stated, Kremlin officials turned to Russian President Vladimir Putin with a request to “rein in” Prigozhin, who criticized the Russian Ministry of Defense. Gershkovich was also one of the authors of a high-profile WSJ article about how Putin’s entourage may be hiding truthful information from him about the war in Ukraine. Putin receives a written report from the front every morning, however, the reports emphasize Russia army’s successes, and failures are tuned down. The reports are also delayed for several days, because they have to pass filters of the FSB and the Security Council, as well as get a personal stamp of approval from Nikolai Patrushev (then the secretary of Russia’s Security Council), the article claimed. Gershkovich's materials before his arrest in March 2023 were devoted to the worsening prospects for the Russian economy, the situation around Bakhmut, the visit to Moscow of China’s leader Xi Jinping and protests over the bill on "foreign agents" in Georgia. According to the photographer who worked with Gershkovich, he was collecting material for an article about how people in Russian regions perceive the war, for which he visited Yekaterinburg and Nizhny Tagil, and planned to go to other cities. Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact: German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop (left), Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and USSR Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov (right) on August 23, 1939 in the Kremlin after signing the pact. Stalin made a toast after the ceremony: "I know how much the German people love their Fuhrer. Therefore, I want to drink to his health." On September 1, 1939 Germany’s attacked Poland. The Soviet Union attacked Poland on September 17, 1939. On September 22, Nazis and Soviets held a joint parade in Brest, celebrating their victory. For 50 years, the USSR leaders denied that there was a secret appendix to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. In 1946, at the Nuremberg Trials, the former State Secretary of the German Foreign Ministry, Ernst von Weizsäcker, spoke about the existence of a secret additional protocol between the USSR and Germany. This was confirmed by other defendants, and one of the lawyers even wanted to read the text of this protocol, but he was not allowed: the USSR representatives called it a fake and said such a document never existed. In 1948, the secret protocol, based on photocopies of the German original that had not survived, was published in the US State Department collection "Nazi-Soviet Relations. 1939-1941". It also included the correspondence between Nazi and Soviet diplomats, which contained references to secret agreements. But the Soviet Union continued to claim that this was a falsification, that no additional secret appendix to the 1939 agreements ("On Non-Aggression" and "On Friendship and Borders") between the USSR and Germany existed. Moreover: in response to the publication by the State Department, Moscow published its own work titled "Falsifiers of History". But it did not contain a single complete copy of a document, only a few fragments. Stalin didn’t want to be blamed in starting the World War with Hitler, and used the status of the USSR as one of the “victors of WW2” to suppress this extremely important information. Molotov, who signed the non-aggression pact and the secret protocol to it, denied its existence until his death in 1986. Minister of Foreign Affairs of the USSR Vyacheslav Molotov in Berlin, November 14, 1940. It was hard to prove that such a document existed: one party that signed it (Hitler's Germany) no longer existed, and the other (the Soviet Union) denied that it existed at all, and had no intention of publishing it. Only in 1989, the Soviet leaders admitted that such secret protocol existed, on request of representatives of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. A copy of the German document was published in the USSR. The actual copy of the secret protocol in Russian was first kept in Stalin's safe and then in the archive of the Central Committee of the Communist Party. In 1992, after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the archive of the Communist Party was declassified and the secret protocol was discovered. From that moment, the existence of a secret additional treaty to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact had become a reliably recognized fact not only in the West, not only in the Baltic countries, Moldova and Ukraine, but also in Russia itself. But now, Putin’s propaganda downplays the importance of the secret agreement between Hitler and Stalin how they would divide Europe, and overemphasizes that it was a non-aggression pact, which allowed the USSR 2 more years without the war. The legend of Kyiv being founded in 482 by brothers Kyi, Shchek, Khoryv and their sister Lybid was also included. By adopting the name “Rossia” (Russia) Muscovy princes laid their claim on the lands that belonged to Ukraine. 1709 newspaper “The Daily Courant” talks about Muscovy and Ukraine.
